analysis.note: The final visarga is elided before initial e in enam.
Masculine singular object, referring to the Self; final m appears as anusvāra before v.
The commentary glosses vetti with vijānāti.
Predicative accusative with enam: ‘as the slayer’; the commentary identifies it as the agent of the act of killing.
The visarga becomes ś before c.
This analysis shares the printed sandhi-token cainaṃ with the following enam; ca + enam yields cainam.
This analysis shares the printed sandhi-token cainaṃ with preceding ca; it is the object of manyate and is qualified predicatively by hatam.
Ātmanepada form in active, or Kartari, construction.
A kta-participial stem used as a predicative accusative with enam: ‘as slain.’
Dual pronominal adjective referring jointly to the two persons introduced by the relative clauses.
Correlative pronoun answering the two preceding instances of yaḥ.
The dual agrees with ubhau tau; final -aḥ becomes -o before the following n.
This analysis shares the printed sandhi-token nāyaṃ with following ayam; na + ayam yields nāyam.
This analysis shares the printed sandhi-token nāyaṃ with preceding na; it denotes the Self discussed in the preceding clauses.
Active: the commentary expressly denies that the Self is the agent of killing.
Passive: the commentary expressly denies that the Self becomes the patient of killing.

justifications.decision: The pronouns enam and ayam denote the presently discussed Self (ātman), described as the embodied one (dehin), not the physical body itself.
Hantāram and hatam are predicative accusatives qualifying enam: the first presents the Self as agent of killing, while the second presents it as the patient who has been slain.
options_considered: ordinary direct objects independent of enam
predicative accusatives expressing agent and patient roles
appositional names without reference to killing roles
justifications.chosen: predicative accusatives: ‘as the slayer’ and ‘as slain’

evidence.quote: hantāraṃ hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartāraṃ ya ca enam anyo manyate hataṃ deha-hananena hato 'ham iti hanana-kriyāyāḥ karma-bhūtam
evidence.translation: ‘Hantāram: the agent of the act of killing; and another regards this as slain—“I have been slain through the killing of the body”—as having become the patient of the act of killing.’

justifications.decision: Ubhau tau gathers the subjects of both relative clauses into one dual subject, and na vijānītaḥ denies them genuine understanding of the Self rather than all cognition whatsoever.
options_considered: only the second person is denied knowledge
both persons lack genuine knowledge of the Self
the two persons know two different truths
justifications.chosen: both persons fail to understand the Self’s true nature

evidence.quote: tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam
evidence.translation: ‘Those two, both, do not understand—have not known—the Self, because of non-discrimination.’
‘The meaning is that those two are unacquainted with the Self’s true nature.’

justifications.decision: Hanti is active and denies the Self the status of agent; hanyate is passive and denies it the status of patient. Both denials are grounded in the Self’s immutability.
options_considered: hanyate as a general statement that the Self does not perish
an explicit active/passive denial of agency and patienthood
justifications.chosen: ‘neither slays nor is slain,’ denying agency and patienthood

evidence.quote: hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt
hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt
evidence.translation: ‘[It] slays not: it does not become the agent of the act of killing; nor is it slain, and so does not become the patient—the meaning being that it is immutable.’

justifications.decision: The two mistaken judgments are first-person identifications—‘I am the slayer’ and ‘I have been slain’—arising when bodily killing is superimposed upon the Self.
options_considered: literal and true predicates of the body
first-person misidentifications of the Self with bodily agency or injury
justifications.chosen: first-person misidentification caused by failure to discriminate body and Self

evidence.quote: hantā ahaṃ, hato 'smy aham iti deha-hananena ātmānam ahaṃ pratyaya-viṣayaṃ yau vijānītaḥ
evidence.translation: ‘The two who cognize the Self, the object of the “I”-notion, as “I am the slayer” and “I have been slain,” on account of the killing of the body.’

translation:
Whoever knows this Self (ātman) as the slayer, and whoever regards it as slain—
both of them fail to understand: this Self neither slays nor is slain.
one_shot_delta: A commentary-blind translation might take enam and ayam as referring to the physical body; Śaṅkara identifies their referent as the Self and treats bodily killing as the source of the error.
It might read the first two clauses as valid descriptions, whereas the commentary says that both thinkers lack discrimination and do not know the Self’s true nature.
It might render hanyate merely as ‘does not perish’ or as a middle form; the commentary specifically construes it passively and denies that the Self is the patient of killing.
It might miss the first-person force of the error: Śaṅkara expands the judgments as ‘I am the slayer’ and ‘I have been slain.’
mula: ya enaṃ vetti hantāraṃ yaś cainaṃ manyate hatam | ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṃ hanti na hanyate
commentary_lines: ya enaṃ prakṛtaṃ dehinaṃ vetti vijānāti hantāraṃ hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartāraṃ ya ca enam anyo manyate hataṃ deha-hananena hato 'ham iti hanana-kriyāyāḥ karma-bhūtam |
tau ubhau na vijānītaḥ na jñātavantau avivekena ātmānam |
hantā ahaṃ, hato 'smy aham iti deha-hananena ātmānam ahaṃ pratyaya-viṣayaṃ yau vijānītaḥ tau ātma-svarūpānabhijñau ity arthaḥ |
yasmāt na ayam atmā hanti na hanana-kriyāyāḥ kartā bhavati, na ca hanyate na ca karma bhavatīty arthaḥ, avikriyatvāt ||bhgs_2.19||
